title: Fixing instead of throwing away: Africa’s overlooked green industrial advantage
body:
While many advanced economies are trying to build circular economies through policy frameworks and industrial strategies, Africa has been operating one organically for decades

Walk through many African cities and you will notice something remarkable

Phones are repaired rather than discarded

Appliances are fixed rather than replaced

Vehicle components are reused and rebuilt rather than thrown away

These are not niche activities. They are a core part of everyday economic life in Africa

But here is the paradox: Africa's repair ecosystems are rarely recognized as part of industrial policy. At best, they are often treated as survivalist activities rather than understood for what they truly are: productive economic infrastructure that supports resource efficiency, employment, and technological learning

The result: Africa’s large repair ecosystems remain informal, decentralized, and driven by small-scale entrepreneurs

This needs to change

Green industrialization is not only about low-carbon energy systems, industrial decarbonization, or manufacturing green technologies. It is also about resource efficiency and circular economic models, of which the repair economy is an essential component

Africa’s continued neglect of this ecosystem therefore represents a missed bottom-up opportunity for green industrialization

So what needs to happen? With the right support, repair ecosystems could evolve from fragmented informal markets into organized clusters that support circular manufacturing and industrial upgrading

Three policy shifts are needed to unlock this potential

- Support repair clusters in urban and rural markets. Providing infrastructure, workspace, reliable electricity, and improved logistics would allow technicians and small firms to scale operation and increase productivity.
- Invest in skills development for repair technicians. Training and certification programs in electronics, diagnostics, and refurbishment technologies would strengthen technical capabilities and create pathways toward assembly activities, remanufacturing, and light manufacturing.
- Introduce right-to-repair frameworks that guarantee access to spare parts, repair manuals, and diagnostic tools.

**Bottom line:** Africa’s green industrialization does not have to start from scratch—or begin with complex new systems.

Sometimes the first step toward green industrialization is very simple: Fixing what already exists. This already exists in repair markets, workshops, and technician networks across many African countries.

The real opportunity now is to upgrade and integrate this repair ecosystems into broader green industrial transformation agenda.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Woubet Kassa Solomon Owusu Emmanuel Buadi Mensah
